idiom_name: internal implementation plus a narrow internal attorney type; file-scoped types for source-level grants and InternalsVisibleTo for exactly one friend assembly
implementation_notes: C# has no friend-to-type declaration: private is per class (a nested type can reach the enclosing type's private members), internal is assembly-wide, file restricts a top-level type to its source file, and an assembly can name its friends with [assembly: InternalsVisibleTo] (Microsoft Learn, access modifiers and friend assemblies). The attorney therefore takes the shape the assembly model allows: keep the implementation internal or file (so it is not public API) and expose a small internal attorney type whose members are the only granted entry points; when the collaborator lives in another assembly, InternalsVisibleTo hands it the internal surface - genuinely selective, but assembly-granular, and the closest thing C# has to friendship. Reach for the hand-built attorney when the grant must be narrower than 'this assembly': there the narrowness comes from the attorney's own surface and from review, not from the compiler.
pitfalls: internal is assembly-granular, so inside the assembly the attorney's narrow surface is a convention: any type in that assembly can call Grid.Recalc directly.

[InternalsVisibleTo] names an assembly, so anyone who can build an assembly with that identity receives the whole internal surface; when the granting assembly is strong named, the friend name must carry the public key of the helper's key pair.

There is no friend-to-type, so a helper outside the class cannot be given access to private members at all - do not 'solve' that by making the members public; widen to internal plus InternalsVisibleTo, or restructure the types.
